views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go to the G20 meeting in Argentina prepared to seek a pause on new escalation — specifically to defer the scheduled Jan 1, 2019 rise in US tariffs on $200B of our goods from 10% to 25%, and to head off the threatened additional $267B in tariffs that would cover virtually all our exports — in exchange for a credible, limited package (e.g., increased purchases of US goods) rather than sweeping structural concessions. Hold our retaliation posture in reserve and avoid repeating the May truce mistake of unilateral capitulation; use the recent Trump-Xi dialogue as the off-ramp, not as a reason to relax.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is high and grounded in macro evidence. Our manufacturing PMI fell to 50.2 in October, a 27-month low, with new export orders contracting for a fifth straight month to 46.9, and mid/small firms already in contraction — the first full month of the $200B tariffs and a clear sign the export engine is weakening (Caixin, CNBC, Politico, 2018-10-31). GDP grew only 6.5% in Q3, the weakest since Q1 2009, and the yuan slid toward 7/USD, a 21-month low (Washington Post, 2018-10-18). The clock is the real threat: the $200B tariff rises to 25% on Jan 1 and Trump has threatened $267B more (Politico, 2018-11-01), so 'front-loading' exporters will see orders collapse in January. That is a +0.5 high-threat, export-sector and FX-pressure situation, not yet existential (large reserves, no CCP-legitimacy or financial-stability crisis), hence not +1.0. The action stance is mild de-escalation toward negotiation precisely because the costs of escalation now are asymmetric and bad for us: raising the stakes risks triggering the Jan 1 hike and the $267B tranche at a moment our cyclical data is already deteriorating. The Nov 1 Trump-Xi phone call — both leaders upbeat, a G20 meeting scheduled, talks reportedly 'moving along nicely' and Trump asking officials to draft terms (Reuters/Globe and Mail, 2018-11-02) — opens a genuine off-ramp. We should use that summit to secure a pause and a truce in exchange for limited purchase commitments, while keeping our retaliatory options and avoiding unilateral structural reforms before the US makes a matching commitment.
key_factors: China October manufacturing PMI at 27-month low of 50.2; export orders contracting 5 straight months
Q3 GDP growth 6.5%, weakest since Q1 2009
Jan 1, 2019 US tariff hike on $200B of our goods to 25% plus threatened additional $267B
Trump-Xi Nov 1 phone call; G20 presidential meeting scheduled late Nov — off-ramp available
Export 'front-loading' implies sharp order/production drop in January
